title: Episode 107: Queen Liliuokalani: The Overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom
description:
In January 1893, Queen Liliuokalani fought to restore democratic power to her native Hawaiian people. Backed by United States Marines, a cabal of wealthy American sugar planters overthrew the sovereign Hawaiian monarchy, sparking a century of struggle for Hawaiian sovereignty.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the grand, elegant halls of ʻIolani Palace in Honolulu, Hawaii, to witness one of the most heartbreaking, controversial, and shameful acts of imperial aggression in nineteenth-century history: the illegal overthrow of Queen Liliuokalani and the Kingdom of Hawaii in January eighteen ninety-three. Highly educated, musically gifted, and deeply beloved by her people, Queen Liliuokalani ascended the throne determined to overturn the humiliating, coerced 'Bayonet Constitution' and restore democratic voting rights to native Hawaiians. But standing against her was a ruthless cabal of American sugar oligarchs, backed by the unauthorized military power of United States Marines. Rather than spill the blood of her people, the Queen yielded her authority under protest to the United States government, trusting in American justice. What followed was a tragic struggle that culminated in her house arrest in her own palace, composing the immortal farewell song 'Aloha ʻOe.' Here is George with the full, poignant chronicle.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE SCHOLAR-QUEEN AND THE GARDEN OF MUSIC
Born Lydia Liliʻu Loloku Walania Wewehi Kamakaʻeha on September second, eighteen thirty-eight, into one of Hawaii's highest aliʻi noble families, Queen Liliuokalani was an extraordinary woman of intellect, artistic brilliance, and profound spiritual depth. Raised in accordance with traditional Hawaiian hānai custom, she was formally educated alongside future monarchs at the Royal School by American Protestant missionaries, mastering English, Latin, mathematics, and European royal protocol.
Liliuokalani was a gifted musical virtuoso who played the organ, piano, and guitar, composing over one hundred and fifty sacred hymns and traditional mele chants that remain treasured cornerstones of Hawaiian cultural heritage. Her most celebrated composition, written in eighteen seventy-eight following a horseback ride on Oʻahu, was 'Aloha ʻOe'—'Farewell to Thee'—a hauntingly beautiful melody whose poignant lyrics of parting lovers would later become the tragic anthem of a stolen nation.
In eighteen ninety-one, upon the death of her beloved brother, King David Kalākaua, Liliuokalani took the royal oath inside ʻIolani Palace, ascending the throne as the eighth and final monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom. She inherited a proud, internationally recognized sovereign nation that had treaties of friendship with over twenty foreign powers, including the United States, Great Britain, France, and Imperial Germany. Yet beneath the glittering surface of the royal court, a deadly political cancer was consuming the kingdom's sovereignty. Liliuokalani's deep Christian faith and mastery of Western literature, diplomacy, and classical music made her one of the most intellectually accomplished monarchs of the Victorian era.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SINS OF THE BAYONET CONSTITUTION
The primary threat to Hawaiian sovereignty came from a small, wealthy minority of white American and European missionary descendants, merchants, and sugar barons who dominated the islands' agricultural economy. Under lucrative trade reciprocity treaties with the United States, immense sugar plantations boomed across the islands, generating colossal fortunes for American oligarchs like Sanford B. Dole, Lorrin Thurston, and the Big Five trading conglomerates.
However, the planters were not content with economic dominance; they demanded total political control. In July eighteen eighty-seven, a secretive paramilitary organization of white merchants known as the Honolulu Rifles staged an armed coup d'état against King Kalākaua. Cornering the king in his palace at gunpoint, they forced him to sign the humiliating 'Bayonet Constitution.'
The Bayonet Constitution stripped the Hawaiian monarchy of virtually all executive power, transforming the king into a powerless figurehead. Worse still, it established exorbitant property and income requirements for voting, disenfranchising over seventy-five percent of native Hawaiian citizens and all Asian residents, while granting the vote to foreign American and European residents who refused to take an oath of allegiance to Hawaii. Native Hawaiians watched in anguish as control of their own government was stolen by a wealthy foreign minority. The Bayonet Constitution represented a blatant, armed coup by foreign commercial interests determined to subjugate native sovereignty for private agricultural profits.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE CRY OF THE PEOPLE FOR A NEW CONSTITUTION
When Queen Liliuokalani ascended the throne in eighteen ninety-one, native Hawaiian citizens flooded ʻIolani Palace with over six thousand petitions signed in every district across the islands, begging the Queen to promulgate a new constitution that would abolish the Bayonet Constitution and restore their democratic franchise.
Liliuokalani recognized that continuing the minority rule of foreign sugar planters would inevitably lead to the total economic and cultural subjugation of her people. She drafted a proposed constitution that restored royal executive authority, reduced voting property qualifications, and strictly limited the vote to Hawaiian citizens. It was a constitution that was supported by an overwhelming ninety percent of the kingdom's populace.
On Saturday afternoon, January fourteenth, eighteen ninety-three, following the formal prorogation of the legislative assembly, the Queen prepared to sign the new constitution inside ʻIolani Palace. However, her cabinet ministers—intimidated by threats of violence from white merchants—hesitated and pleaded with the Queen to delay the proclamation. Recognizing that proceeding without unified cabinet support could provoke civil strife, Liliuokalani reluctantly postponed the signing, addressing thousands of disappointed Hawaiian subjects gathered on the palace lawn, promising that their rights would soon be restored. Over ninety percent of native Hawaiian citizens signed emotional petitions begging their Queen to restore the sacred democratic rights stolen by the missionary sugar oligarchy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CONSPIRACY AND THE LANDING OF THE MARINES
The Queen's attempt to restore democratic governance provided the pretext that the American sugar oligarchs had long been waiting for. A cabal of thirteen white businessmen, led by attorney Lorrin Thurston, immediately formed the treasonous 'Committee of Safety.' Their goal was not merely to stop the new constitution, but to overthrow the sovereign Hawaiian monarchy and annex the islands to the United States, allowing Hawaiian sugar to enter the American market free of McKinley Tariff penalties.
Crucial to the conspiracy was John L. Stevens, the United States Minister to Hawaii. Stevens was a fervent, expansionist imperialist who had previously written to the State Department describing Hawaii as a 'ripe pear' ready to be plucked by the American eagle. Working in direct conspiracy with the Committee of Safety, Stevens took a treasonous step: on Monday afternoon, January sixteenth, eighteen ninety-three, under the false pretense of 'protecting American lives and property,' he ordered United States Navy Captain Gilbert Wiltse to land armed military forces from the cruiser USS Boston anchored in Honolulu Harbor.
One hundred and sixty-two heavily armed United States Marines and sailors, equipped with Gatling guns and field artillery, marched through the streets of Honolulu. Instead of guarding the American legation, the troops took up offensive military positions directly across the street from ʻIolani Palace and the royal government building, training their weapons directly at the Queen's residence in an unmistakable display of military intimidation. The unauthorized landing of United States Marines with Gatling guns and artillery directly outside the royal palace constituted a flagrant act of international military intimidation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: YIELDING UNDER PROTEST: THE QUEEN'S SACRIFICE
On the afternoon of Tuesday, January seventeenth, eighteen ninety-three, the Committee of Safety entered the government building under the protective shadow of American cannons and proclaimed the establishment of a 'Provisional Government of Hawaii,' appointing jurist Sanford B. Dole as president. Minutes later, Minister Stevens committed a flagrant violation of international law by formally recognizing the Provisional Government as the de facto authority of Hawaii, before the Queen had surrendered and while the royal palace remained garrisoned by six hundred loyal royal guards.
The Queen's military commanders and native Hawaiian leaders begged Liliuokalani to allow them to fight. They argued that their six hundred armed guards and thousands of loyal warriors could easily overwhelm the white conspirators. But Liliuokalani was a devout Christian and a devoted mother to her people. She knew that any armed resistance would lead to a bloody massacre by United States Marine artillery, resulting in the slaughter of hundreds of young Hawaiian men and the bombardment of Honolulu.
Choosing moral strength over bloodshed, Queen Liliuokalani issued her historic, formal declaration yielding her authority not to the illegal Provisional Government, but under protest to the United States of America: 'Now to avoid any collision of armed forces, and perhaps the loss of life, I do under this protest, and impelled by said force, yield my authority until such time as the Government of the United States shall, upon facts being presented to it, undo the action of its representative and reinstate me in the authority which I claim as the Constitutional Sovereign of the Hawaiian Islands.' Rather than sacrifice the lives of her young royal guards against American naval artillery, Queen Liliuokalani surrendered her authority under protest, trusting in American justice.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BLOUNT REPORT AND THE REPUBLIC OF HAWAII
Queen Liliuokalani's faith in American constitutional justice was initially vindicated. When President Grover Cleveland took office in Washington in March eighteen ninety-three, he immediately withdrew the annexation treaty submitted by the conspirators, denouncing the overthrow as an act of international piracy. Cleveland dispatched former congressman James H. Blount to Honolulu to conduct an exhaustive, independent investigation.
In July eighteen ninety-three, the historic Blount Report was released. Blount's findings were blistering: he concluded that United States Minister Stevens had conspired with a small minority of foreign planters to execute an illegal armed coup against a friendly, sovereign nation, and that an overwhelming majority of native Hawaiians opposed annexation and supported their Queen. President Cleveland addressed a joint session of Congress, declaring that the overthrow was 'an act of war, committed with the participation of a diplomatic representative of the United States and without authority of Congress,' demanding that the lawful monarch be restored.
However, Sanford Dole and the sugar oligarchs flatly refused to step down, declaring the 'Republic of Hawaii' on July fourth, eighteen ninety-four. In January eighteen ninety-five, loyalist Hawaiian patriots staged an armed counter-revolution to restore their Queen, but the uprising was crushed. Queen Liliuokalani was arrested, subjected to a humiliating military show trial inside her own throne room, and sentenced to five years of hard labor and a five-thousand-dollar fine, later commuted to eight months of strict imprisonment in an upstairs bedroom of ʻIolani Palace. The exhaustive findings of the Blount Report conclusively proved that the Queen had been unlawfully deposed through the treasonous conspiracy of Minister Stevens and foreign planters.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE KŪʻĒ PETITIONS AND THE ETERNAL TORCH OF ALOHA
During her eight months of imprisonment in ʻIolani Palace, denied newspapers and visitors, Queen Liliuokalani displayed breathtaking grace and fortitude. She composed music, hand-stitched an intricate commemorative silk quilt recording the history of her reign, and prayed for her people. In eighteen ninety-seven, following the election of expansionist President William McKinley, a renewed annexation treaty was sent to the United States Senate.
In response, native Hawaiian patriotic organizations mounted one of the most heroic civic resistance campaigns in world history: the Kūʻē Petitions. Traveling by horseback, canoe, and foot across every island, Hawaiian organizers collected the signatures of twenty-one thousand two hundred and sixty-nine native Hawaiian citizens—over ninety percent of the adult native population—formally opposing annexation. Queen Liliuokalani traveled personally to Washington, D.C., presenting the colossal petitions to the United States Senate, successfully killing the annexation treaty.
Yet in eighteen ninety-eight, during the imperial hysteria of the Spanish-American War, McKinley bypassed the constitutional two-thirds treaty requirement, annexing Hawaii via the controversial Newlands Resolution, a simple joint resolution of Congress. Queen Liliuokalani lived out her remaining years at Washington Place in Honolulu, fighting tirelessly for her people's welfare until her death on November eleventh, nineteen seventeen.
In nineteen ninety-three—one hundred years after the coup—the United States Congress passed and President Bill Clinton signed the historic Apology Resolution, formally apologizing to native Hawaiians for the illegal overthrow of their kingdom and the suppression of their inherent sovereignty. Today, Queen Liliuokalani stands as an immortal symbol of dignity, forgiveness, and cultural resilience. Her spirit lives on in every verse of 'Aloha ʻOe,' reminding the world of a sovereign Hawaiian nation that never truly surrendered its soul. The Kūʻē Petitions, containing over twenty-one thousand verified native signatures, stand in the National Archives as a monumental testament to Hawaii's unyielding patriotic resistance.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Queen Liliuokalani's grace, moral dignity, and immortal song 'Aloha ʻOe' continue to inspire the Hawaiian people and lovers of freedom across the globe. That concludes our epic fifty-state journey! I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we inaugurate our new series: the fascinating, untold stories of the Presidents of the United States.
